1.title: THE ISLAND
1.narrative: You are the government. Three islanders -- Alex, Blake, and Casey -- each hunt, fish, build shelter, and gather alone. They produce enough to survive, but barely. Life is subsistence.
1.scenario: A storm destroys Casey's shelter. Alex and Blake could help, but there's no rule about who owns what. Blake asks: should we establish rules about ownership?

economic_terms.definition: Recognized claims over resources and output -- the precondition that makes voluntary exchange possible.
economic_terms.consequence: By establishing property rights, each islander now owns what they produce. This creates the trust needed for trade and specialization in the rounds ahead.
economic_terms.realworld: Countries with strong, enforced property rights -- Singapore, Canada, Switzerland -- consistently see higher investment, longer time horizons, and more specialization than countries without them.

A.text: Establish property rights -- everyone owns what they produce.

B.text: Leave everything open-access -- no ownership rules.

C.text: Grant all property to Alex and Blake only; Casey owns nothing.

2.title: THE TRADE
2.narrative: Blake realizes: "I'm good at fishing. I hate hunting. Alex hates fishing but loves hunting." Blake proposes: "I fish. You hunt. We trade."
2.scenario: The government has a choice: allow this specialization, or require everyone to keep producing everything themselves?

economic_terms.term: Division of Labor, Gains from Trade & Comparative Advantage
economic_terms.definition: Specializing in what you're relatively best at, then trading, makes everyone better off -- even if one party is better at everything.
economic_terms.consequence: By allowing free trade, Blake fishes and Alex hunts full-time instead of doing both badly. Total output rises immediately, and the island discovers gains from trade.
economic_terms.realworld: Adam Smith's pin factory and Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage explain why even small, resource-poor economies like Hong Kong or Switzerland can grow rich through specialization and trade.

C.text: Only allow Alex and Blake to trade; Casey must stay alone.

3.title: GROWTH
3.narrative: Two new people -- Dana and Elliot -- arrive. With 5 people, specialization deepens. Output per person rises 30%. But barter is messy: "I have 20 fish. I want tools. But the tool-maker wants meat, not fish."
3.scenario: The government must decide: adopt a medium of exchange to replace barter?

economic_terms.term: Medium of Exchange, Commodity Money & the Double Coincidence of Wants
economic_terms.definition: A medium of exchange is a good everyone accepts in trade, eliminating the need to find someone who wants exactly what you have (the 'double coincidence of wants').
economic_terms.consequence: By adopting gold as money, trade no longer requires two people to want each other's exact goods. Anyone can sell for gold and buy from someone else entirely. Trade volume triples.
economic_terms.realworld: Gold, silver, cowrie shells, and salt have all served as commodity money throughout history precisely because they solved the double-coincidence problem before paper currency existed.

C.text: Decree paper money -- no gold backing.

4.title: BANKING
4.narrative: Gold works. Trade volume triples. Elliot (the trader) says: "People are burying gold at home. I'll hold it and give them receipts." Elliot opens a bank.
4.scenario: The government must decide: regulate banking, or let it run free?

economic_terms.term: Financial Intermediary, Warehouse Banking & Representative Money
economic_terms.definition: A financial intermediary stores commodity money and issues paper claims ('representative money') redeemable for it -- the origin of banking and the gold standard.
economic_terms.consequence: By licensing Elliot's bank and requiring 50% gold reserves, paper notes stay trustworthy and redeemable. Banking expands trade without abandoning sound money.
economic_terms.realworld: The gold standard, used by most major economies from the 1870s to 1971, worked because notes were reliably redeemable in gold -- reserve requirements existed precisely to protect that trust.

economic_terms.definition: Issuing more paper claims than the reserves actually held -- 'fractional' reserve banking funds booms but risks a collapse in trust.
economic_terms.consequence: By licensing the bank but never enforcing reserves, Elliot issues far more notes than he holds in gold. It works until everyone asks for their gold back at once.
economic_terms.realworld: Nearly every historical banking panic -- the U.S. in 1907 and 1929, and countless emerging-market crises -- traces back to reserves that couldn't cover the claims issued against them.

A.text: License the bank and require reserves (50% gold backing).

B.text: License the bank but never enforce reserves.

5.title: CAPITAL
5.narrative: Casey says: "I want to build a fishing net. It costs 100 gold. I have 50. Can I borrow?" Elliot agrees. Casey builds it. Fishing output explodes 5x.
5.scenario: The government must decide: support entrepreneurs, or suppress them?

economic_terms.definition: Capital investment means giving up consumption today to build a tool that raises output tomorrow. Interest is the price of that trade-off -- the value of time itself.
economic_terms.consequence: By letting Casey borrow to build a fishing net, the island trades 50 gold of present consumption for a tool that multiplies future fishing output five-fold.
economic_terms.realworld: Every industrial economy grew by channeling savings into capital -- factories, machines, infrastructure -- through banks willing to lend against future, not just present, production.

C.text: Only allow the elite to borrow.

6.title: PRODUCTIVITY SURGE
6.narrative: Casey's net works. Blake builds better hooks. Dana makes better ropes. Elliot invents a fish smoker. Tools improve. Costs fall 40%. At lower prices, people buy more.
6.scenario: The government must control inflation: keep the money supply aligned with real output.

economic_terms.definition: When entrepreneurs risk capital on better tools and methods, the same labor produces more output -- shifting supply outward and lowering prices (Schumpeter's 'creative destruction').
economic_terms.consequence: With entrepreneurship supported and reserves enforced, better nets, hooks, ropes, and smokers cut costs 40%. Falling prices raise real wages without printing a single extra coin.
economic_terms.realworld: The Industrial Revolution's productivity gains -- from the spinning jenny to the steam engine -- followed exactly this pattern: entrepreneurs financing tools that lowered costs and raised living standards.

economic_terms.definition: MV = PQ: if the money supply shrinks faster than output grows, prices must fall -- and falling prices can make people hoard cash instead of spending or investing it.
economic_terms.consequence: By over-tightening reserves and shrinking the money supply, prices fall year after year. Islanders delay purchases waiting for even lower prices, and investment dries up.
economic_terms.realworld: Japan's 'Lost Decade' showed how a shrinking money supply can trap a technologically sound economy in a low-output equilibrium for fifteen years or more.

economic_terms.definition: Issuing unlimited notes against limited gold reserves floods the economy with money that isn't backed by real output.
economic_terms.consequence: By letting banks issue unlimited money, credit floods the island faster than fishermen and farmers can produce real goods. Prices spiral upward until trust in money breaks.
economic_terms.realworld: Every hyperinflation on record -- Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe, Venezuela -- began with money issued far faster than real output could grow.

B.text: Over-tighten reserves; shrink the money supply.

C.text: Ignore reserves; let banks issue unlimited money.

7.title: STABILITY
7.narrative: Five years of 7% growth. Real wages up 40%. Island prospers. Pressure appears: the fishing ground is getting crowded. Fish stocks falling. Soon it will collapse.
7.scenario: The government must decide: regulate the fishing ground before collapse, or leave it open?

economic_terms.definition: A resource nobody owns individually gets over-exploited, because no single user bears the full cost of their own use of it.
economic_terms.consequence: By setting fishing quotas now, before the stock collapses, the island avoids the tragedy of the commons entirely. The fishery stays healthy for the rounds ahead.
economic_terms.realworld: Icelandic and Norwegian fisheries, regulated early with enforced quotas, have sustained yields for generations.

economic_terms.definition: A resource nobody owns individually gets over-exploited, because no single user bears the full cost of their own use of it.
economic_terms.consequence: By leaving the fishing ground open, every fisherman fishes harder to get their share before others do. The stock collapses entirely, and the island's food supply goes with it.
economic_terms.realworld: Easter Island's deforestation and collapsed fisheries show what happens when a shared resource has no rules and no enforcement -- total collapse, followed by famine and conflict.

economic_terms.term: Tragedy of the Commons -- Late Regulation
economic_terms.definition: A resource nobody owns individually gets over-exploited, because no single user bears the full cost of their own use of it.
economic_terms.consequence: By waiting until the fishery is already in trouble to impose quotas, the island avoids total collapse -- but stocks fall hard first, and recovery takes decades.
economic_terms.realworld: Iceland's North Atlantic cod fishery crashed in the 1970s despite warning signs; quotas imposed only after the crash brought partial recovery, but only after a lost decade.

B.text: Leave it open; let people fish freely.

8.title: PROTECTED COMMONS
8.narrative: Government sets quotas. Each person fishes at most 200 fish/year, with heavy fines for violations. Five years later, fish populations are stable. A merchant ship appears -- from another island with tropical fruit, spices, and copper.
8.scenario: The government must decide: open external trade, or stay closed?

economic_terms.term: External Trade, Comparative Advantage at Scale & Exchange Rates
economic_terms.definition: The logic of specialization and trade applies between whole communities, not just individuals -- but trading across currencies requires a working exchange-rate mechanism.
economic_terms.consequence: By opening trade freely with the other island, both economies specialize further -- yours in processed fish, theirs in fruit and spices -- and both sides get richer.
economic_terms.realworld: Post-war trade liberalization between economies like South Korea and its trading partners followed exactly this logic: open trade let each side specialize in what it did best.

economic_terms.definition: Comparative advantage between communities goes unrealized when there's no working exchange-rate mechanism to translate prices across currencies.
economic_terms.consequence: Trade opens on paper, but with no way to convert gold to the other island's silver at a stable rate, almost no one actually trades. The opportunity sits mostly unused.
economic_terms.realworld: Pre-euro Europe's tangle of currencies -- Deutsche Mark, Franc, Lira, Peseta -- left real comparative advantage unrealized for decades until the 1999 monetary union.

C.text: Open trade, but with no exchange-rate mechanism.

9.title: EXTERNAL TRADE
9.narrative: Ships arrive regularly. Your island specializes in processed fish; the other specializes in fruit. Both prosper. Comparative advantage applies at the island level -- incomes rise 30%. Elliot handles currency exchange between your gold and their silver.
9.scenario: The government faces its final choice: maintain all regulations, or relax them for insiders?

B.text: Relax regulations; let officials exempt insiders.

E1.name: The Prosperous Republic
E1.narrative: All institutions worked in harmony. Property rights, trade, sound money, banking, capital investment, and protected commons combined into decades of exponential growth.
E1.realworld: Singapore: strong property rights, regulated banking, protected commons, open trade. GDP/capita $72,000, 7% growth, low inequality.

E2.name: Prosperous but Insular
E2.narrative: Every internal institution worked perfectly -- but the island closed its doors to outside trade, capping growth well below its true potential.
E2.realworld: Japan (1980s-1990s): world-class manufacturing and banking, but protectionist trade policy limited the growth ceiling. GDP/capita $39,000, 4-5% growth, Gini 0.30.

E3.name: Commons Crisis
E3.narrative: The commons were never protected. Fishing grounds and resources were stripped bare by unrestrained use, and the island's prosperity reversed into catastrophic collapse.
E3.realworld: Easter Island: population collapsed from roughly 15,000 to under 2,000 after deforestation destroyed fishing grounds and food supply -- societal collapse, warfare, starvation.

E4.name: Inflation Crisis
E4.narrative: Money was issued far beyond what gold reserves could back. Trust in currency shattered, hyperinflation destroyed savings, and the island reverted toward barter.
E4.realworld: Venezuela: GDP/capita fell 75% from its peak; hyperinflation hit 2,600% annually in 2020; the currency was reset three times in a decade.

E5.name: Stagnation: No Property Rights
E5.narrative: Without property rights, no one had reason to specialize or trade. The island remained locked in permanent autarky -- everyone producing everything alone, forever.
E5.realworld: North Korea: GDP/capita around $1,300, essentially flat growth since the 1990s, virtually no trade, and only the state holds real claims on output.

E6.name: Extractive Elite State
E6.narrative: Property rights and capital access were granted only to a ruling clique. The elite prospered while most islanders lived at subsistence, propping up wealth they never shared.
E6.realworld: Saudi Arabia (1970s-1990s): oligarchic control of oil wealth by the Al Saud family; moderate aggregate growth masked high inequality and subsistence wages for most.

E7.name: Closed Barter Economy
E7.narrative: Specialization took hold, but without money, every trade required a double coincidence of wants. Growth crawled forward, slow but real, for generations.
E7.realworld: Medieval Europe (pre-1200): craftspeople, knights, and monks specialized, but barter throttled trade volume -- stable, but with a permanently low income ceiling.

E8.name: Fiat Overreach Crisis
E8.narrative: Paper money was decreed into existence with no backing. It worked -- until the first shock, when trust evaporated overnight and the monetary system had to be rebuilt from scratch.
E8.realworld: Argentina (2001-2002): the peso's peg to the dollar collapsed; bank runs drained ATMs and the currency devalued 75% overnight, forcing a monetary policy rethink.

E9.name: Crony Trade
E9.narrative: Trade was opened, but only to a favored subgroup. A connected few captured the gains from specialization while everyone else was locked out.
E9.realworld: Russia (1990s-2020s): oligarchs captured major export industries; ordinary citizens were excluded from capital, licenses, and major trade -- the top 1% holds 35% of wealth.

E10.name: Capital Starvation
E10.narrative: Banking was banned outright. With no way to borrow, no one could finance new tools, and productivity stayed stuck at subsistence levels.
E10.realworld: Papua New Guinea (modern): under 10% of the population has banking access; credit markets are virtually nonexistent, blocking capital investment.

E11.name: Failed Entrepreneurship
E11.narrative: Entrepreneurs were taxed and licensed into irrelevance. New tools and methods stopped appearing, and productivity flatlined while the rest of the world raced ahead.
E11.realworld: Soviet Union (1960s-1980s): entrepreneurship was effectively illegal; productivity stagnated after the 1970s and the economy could not compete technologically.

E12.name: Demand Collapse
E12.narrative: Productivity surged, but the system meant to turn output into consumption broke down. Goods piled up unsold, producers lost incentive, and shortages appeared despite abundance.
E12.realworld: Soviet Union (1990-1991): perestroika loosened prices and production surged temporarily, but the collapse of central planning meant real output fell 14% as demand collapsed and rationing began.

E13.name: Isolationist Relapse
E13.narrative: The government mandated self-sufficiency quotas and dismantled specialization. Trade networks were torn apart in the name of self-reliance, and the island reverted to autarky under famine conditions.
E13.realworld: China's Cultural Revolution (1966-1976): Mao's communes ordered village-level self-sufficiency, dismantling specialization; the resulting Great Famine killed tens of millions.

E14.name: Fragmented Currencies
E14.narrative: External trade opened, but with no shared exchange-rate mechanism, price signals never translated cleanly across currencies. Trade stayed well below its true potential.
E14.realworld: Pre-EU Europe (1970s-1980s): the Deutsche Mark, Franc, Lira, and Peseta floated against each other with volatile exchange rates, leaving comparative advantage unrealized until the 1999 euro launch.

E15.name: Overexploited Commons
E15.narrative: The commons were regulated only after overuse had already done serious damage. Quotas eventually stabilized the fishery, but recovery took decades and cost a generation of growth.
E15.realworld: Iceland (1970s-2000s): cod stocks crashed despite warnings; quotas imposed in the 1980s brought a 50% stock recovery by 2000, but only after a lost decade of depression and emigration.

E16.name: Regulatory Capture
E16.narrative: On paper, every rule was in place. In practice, officials quietly exempted connected insiders. Growth looks as strong as the best-run economies -- but the foundation is hollow.
E16.realworld: China (2000s-present): state-owned enterprises are often exempt from rules applied to private firms; aggregate growth looks like ~9% GDP growth, but hidden extraction and captured regulation build fragility beneath the surface.

E17.name: Hyper-Deflation
E17.narrative: The money supply was shrunk too far. Prices fell year after year, people hoarded cash waiting for further declines, and investment dried up despite otherwise sound institutions.
E17.realworld: Japan's Lost Decade (1990s-2000s): prices fell 1-2% annually for 15+ years; consumers delayed spending, firms couldn't profitably borrow even near zero rates, and growth stagnated around 0.5%.

E18.name: Subsistence Equilibrium with Limited Trade
E18.narrative: Every institution was built with care -- property rights, banking, capital formation, protected commons -- but trade opened only gradually. The result was steady, realistic prosperity rather than a spectacular boom.
E18.realworld: South Korea (1960s-1980s): property rights, banking, and capital formation all functioning; commons regulated early; modest, gradually opening trade; solid ~6% annual growth -- a stable, mixed-outcome economy.
